findings.title: Monitor server has no cleanup on process exit
findings.detail: The `monitorServer` reference returned by `startMonitorServer()` is captured in a local variable inside the `if (!NO_MONITOR && !_monitorStarted)` block but never stored anywhere after `_monitorStarted = true`. The existing `registerOtelShutdown()` handler (lines 633-646) calls `process.exit(0)` after shutting down OTel on SIGINT/SIGTERM, but it never calls `monitorServer.stop()`. The `MonitorServer` interface exposes a `stop()` method (types.ts:90) which calls `serverInstance.close()` on the underlying Hono/node-server handle (server.ts:481-486). Without calling `stop()`, the HTTP server holds open file-descriptor/socket state and the `setInterval` polling loop inside `/events/stream` (server.ts:112) is never cleared. In practice Node will force-exit the process anyway, but any lingering sockets can delay the process exit and leave OS-level port bindings held momentarily after the MCP stdio server exits. Fix: store `monitorServer` at module scope (or pass it into `registerOtelShutdown`) and call `await monitorServer.stop()` inside the SIGINT/SIGTERM handler before `process.exit(0)`.

findings.title: Port conflict on monitor auto-start is silently swallowed
findings.detail: The entire monitor startup block is wrapped in `try/catch` with non-fatal handling. If port 4721 is already in use (e.g. a previous MCP session still holding it, or another process), `server.start()` throws `EADDRINUSE`. The catch block logs `[fulcrum] Monitor auto-start failed (non-fatal): ...` to stderr, sets `_monitorStarted = false` (the assignment at line 1067 never ran), and continues. This is intentional by design. However, the consequence is that on the next call to `runServeMcp()` — e.g. in tests, or if the parent process restarts the MCP server without restarting the whole process — `_monitorStarted` stays `false` and the code will retry the port bind again, fail again, and log another non-fatal warning. While not a crash, repeated retries produce noisy stderr. A more important issue: `runServeAll()` (line 1285) calls `startMonitorServer()` with no explicit port argument, relying on the `config.port ?? 4721` default, but the auto-start path in `runServeMcp` uses `parseInt(process.env['FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT'] ?? '4721', 10)`. If `FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT` is set and `config.port` is also set to a different value, `runServeAll` and `runServeMcp` disagree on which port to bind. Minor but possible inconsistency.

findings.title: parseInt(FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT) returns NaN on invalid input, NaN passed to startMonitorServer
findings.detail: `const monitorPort = parseInt(process.env['FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT'] ?? '4721', 10)` — if `FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT` is set to a non-numeric value (e.g. `invalid`, `true`, empty string `''`), `parseInt` returns `NaN`. `NaN` is then passed as `port` to `startMonitorServer({ port: NaN })`. Inside server.ts (line 33), `config.port ?? 7331` — `NaN ?? 7331` evaluates to `NaN` (because `NaN` is not `null`/`undefined`), so `port = NaN`. The Hono `serve()` call (server.ts:479) receives `port: NaN` which on Node.js (via `@hono/node-server`) will either silently bind to port 0 (OS-assigned ephemeral port) or throw. Either outcome is incorrect: the monitor silently runs on an unknown port, `probeMonitor` hits the wrong URL, and `monitor_running` in `get_current_context` always returns `false` — with no diagnostic message. Fix: validate with `Number.isFinite(monitorPort)` and fall back to `4721` with a warning.

findings.title: probeMonitor has no in-flight deduplication — thundering herd on cache miss
findings.detail: If multiple concurrent `get_current_context` calls arrive while the cache is empty or expired, each call independently executes `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(200) })` before any of them can populate the cache. With 200ms timeout and the monitor being slow to start, all N concurrent callers will each open a TCP connection and wait up to 200ms. After the first resolves, the cache is populated and subsequent calls within the 15s TTL hit the fast path. The burst is bounded (200ms, then all resolve), so this is unlikely to cause real problems in practice, but in an environment where `get_current_context` is called in parallel (e.g. multiple tool calls during model warm-up), the connection burst could trigger OS rate-limiting on loopback or confuse the monitor's access logging. Fix: use a pending-promise map to coalesce in-flight probes for the same URL.

findings.title: spawnSync timeout on seed data: child killed with SIGTERM but stdout may be empty — no signal check
findings.detail: Node.js `spawnSync` does accept a `timeout` option (milliseconds) — this is correct. On timeout expiry, the child is sent `killSignal` (default `SIGTERM`). The code then checks `ctxChild.stdout` and parses responses, but it does NOT check `ctxChild.signal` or `ctxChild.status`. If the MCP server takes more than 5000ms (e.g. embedding warm-up on first run), `ctxChild.signal` will be `'SIGTERM'`, `ctxChild.stdout` will be whatever was written before the kill, and `ctxChild.stderr` may contain partial output. The code will see `ctxStdout = ''` (or truncated), fail to parse `workspaceId`, and fall through to log `seed memory skipped (best-effort)`. This is the intended fallback, but the user gets no indication that a timeout occurred — only `seed memory skipped (best-effort)` in the output. A check like `if (ctxChild.signal) warn('seed MCP call timed out')` would make timeout failures visible.

findings.title: _monitorStarted module flag does not reset between runServeMcp() calls — breaks test isolation
findings.detail: `let _monitorStarted = false` is module-level. In ESM, module state is cached per module per process. In test environments that call `runServeMcp()` multiple times within the same process (e.g. using `--runInBand` Jest/Vitest, or if tests import the CLI module), the first call sets `_monitorStarted = true` and all subsequent calls skip the monitor block entirely — even if they're meant to test the auto-start behavior. There is no reset mechanism. This is latent: tests that currently run in separate processes are unaffected, but the pattern creates a hidden coupling between test ordering and monitor behavior. The `_otelWarmed`, `_embeddingWarmed`, `_otelShutdownRegistered` flags share the same pattern. Fix: either accept the module-level flag as a deliberate design (document it), or export a `_resetForTests()` function.

findings.title: fulcrum-mcp wrapper auto-starts monitor with no escape hatch documented
findings.detail: The zero-install wrapper `fulcrum-mcp` splices `serve mcp` into `process.argv` and delegates to `@fulcrum/cli`. This means the monitor auto-start fires unconditionally (unless the end-user knows to set `FULCRUM_NO_MONITOR=1` or pass `--no-monitor`). The `claude_desktop_config.json` integration guide and MCP server entry points do not document these escape hatches. If a user runs `fulcrum-mcp` inside a container or restricted network environment where port 4721 is occupied, they will see a non-fatal error on stderr that MCP clients (e.g. Claude Desktop) may surface as a connection warning. This is not a crash, but it creates confusion.

findings.title: writeSeedData second spawnSync skips if workspaceId is empty string — silent no-op
findings.detail: The guard `if (workspaceId)` treats an empty string as falsy. `currentProjectIds()` always returns a deterministic non-empty `workspace_id` based on the CWD hash, so in practice this is fine. However, if the MCP response parsing fails to extract `workspace_id` (due to response format change, JSON nesting, or timeout), `workspaceId` stays `''`, the write step is silently skipped, and `ok('write path validated: ..., seed memory skipped (best-effort)')` is printed — indistinguishable from an intentional skip. There is no way for the user to know whether the skip was because the write worked previously or because the MCP call failed.

residual_risks.title: Monitor holds open HTTP server handle — may delay process exit
residual_risks.detail: Because `monitorServer.stop()` is never called on process exit, the underlying Node.js HTTP server keeps the event loop alive. Node will only exit once the socket is idle/closed (or via `process.exit(0)` from the SIGTERM handler). The SIGTERM handler does call `process.exit(0)` unconditionally, so in practice the process exits cleanly on SIGTERM. The risk is only if the process receives neither SIGINT nor SIGTERM (e.g. parent process dies, causing SIGHUP) — in that case the MCP stdio loop ends but the HTTP server keeps the process alive indefinitely.

residual_risks.title: Double-probe window between TTL expiry and cache repopulation
residual_risks.detail: The probe TTL is 15 seconds. In a long-running session where the monitor goes down and comes back, the first `get_current_context` call after TTL expiry will probe the live monitor and cache `running: true`. If the monitor goes down immediately after, the next 15 seconds of calls will incorrectly report `monitor_running: true`. This is by-design caching trade-off but worth noting for observability.

residual_risks.title: writeSeedData spawns fulcrum with embedding warm-up — may reliably timeout on first install
residual_risks.detail: Each `spawnSync('fulcrum', ['serve', 'mcp'], { timeout: 5000 })` triggers `runServeMcp()` which calls `warmEmbedding()` — potentially downloading or loading a large embedding model for the first time. On slow machines or first-install (cold model cache), this easily exceeds 5 seconds. The timeout is fine for the intent (best-effort), but users on slow machines will always see `seed memory skipped` on first install. A note in the install output would reduce support burden.

testing_gaps.title: No test for NaN port path
testing_gaps.detail: No test exercises `FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT=invalid` to verify the NaN guard behavior (or lack thereof). A unit test that sets `FULCRUM_MONITOR_PORT=bad` and calls `runServeMcp()` with `--no-monitor` to confirm it doesn't crash, plus a test that exercises the parseInt+NaN path directly, would catch R-03.

testing_gaps.title: No test for concurrent probeMonitor calls
testing_gaps.detail: There is no test that fires multiple concurrent `get_current_context` calls to verify the cache prevents N concurrent fetch probes. A test with `Promise.all([...Array(10)].map(() => handleToolCall('get_current_context', {})))` while mocking fetch would document the current behavior and catch regressions if deduplication is added.

testing_gaps.title: No test for spawnSync timeout signal path in writeSeedData
testing_gaps.detail: There is no test that injects a slow MCP server (or mocks spawnSync to return `{ signal: 'SIGTERM', stdout: '' }`) to verify the timeout fallback path. The fallback produces `seed memory skipped (best-effort)` whether the timeout is benign or caused by a misconfiguration — a test would confirm the diagnostic output.

testing_gaps.title: No test for monitor cleanup on SIGTERM
testing_gaps.detail: There is no integration test that starts `runServeMcp()`, sends SIGTERM, and verifies the monitor port is released. Such a test would catch the missing `monitorServer.stop()` call in the shutdown handler (R-01).

testing_gaps.title: No test for _monitorStarted flag isolation between runServeMcp() calls
testing_gaps.detail: No test calls `runServeMcp()` twice in the same module scope to verify the flag prevents double-start. This is the scenario most likely to cause hidden test pollution.
